name: Check-in
intent: The same short page at every return, so change is visible by flipping back.
when: a recurring return to the same question (the Ritual page)

variants.label: Add one line of gratitude
variants.prompt: Rate the rows, say what changed since last time, write one line of gratitude, then write for a few minutes.

claims.claim: Monitoring progress towards a goal increases goal attainment, and more so when the progress is physically recorded.

People recall their earlier attitudes, feelings or confidence as closer to their present state than they were, or as fitting their theory of how they must have changed. A written baseline is therefore needed to see real change.
claims.construct: consistency and change biases in autobiographical memory (implicit theories of stability and change)

claims.claim: Writing about emotional experiences produces small improvements in wellbeing and health outcomes compared with neutral writing.
Regularly writing down things one is grateful for produces small improvements in well-being. Weekly writing is at least as effective as daily.
claims.construct: gratitude interventions; hedonic adaptation to repeated positive activities

grounding.helps: when you want the weekly page to note something that went well: a short gratitude list raised positive mood in controlled studies that used weekly or daily lists, and any gain is likely small
grounding.backfires: when gratitude is forced or rote, or treated as a remedy for low mood, which is why the row is optional and off by default; its benefit over other positive writing is not established

prompt: Rate the rows, say what changed since last time, then write for a few minutes.
readback: Compare with the previous check-ins, not with an ideal. What recurs across returns matters more than any one page. A line that goes rote or empty is itself a signal.

People recall their earlier attitudes, feelings or confidence as closer to their present state than they were, or as fitting their theory of how they must have changed. A written baseline is therefore needed to see real change.
claims.construct: consistency and change biases in autobiographical memory (implicit theories of stability and change)

claims.claim: Writing about emotional experiences produces small improvements in wellbeing and health outcomes compared with neutral writing.
Leaving a visible cue of where you were and what comes next at the point of interruption reduces the time and errors involved in resuming a task.

grounding.helps: when you want to see change over weeks: the same rows written each week are progress monitoring, which gives a small lift to goal attainment, and they keep a baseline your memory would otherwise rewrite; the free-write adds at most a small lift
grounding.backfires: when the rows turn into scores to hit, since rewards tied to a monitored target undermine interest, when the free-write stirs up distress (emotional writing raises it in the short term), or when the ritual becomes a chore and is dropped
